clue.text: Spooner's sweet telegram that's supportive to mugs

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of word pairs, so his name signals that exchange

parts.note: toffee is a sweet; it takes the opening sound of the next word
a cable is an old word for a telegram; it takes the opening sound of the previous word

explanation.surface: Someone receives a telegram of sweet words that are encouraging to gullible people.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the T and C of TOFFEE CABLE gives COFFEE TABLE. 'Mugs' looks like fools; it is cups resting on the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A low table in a living room is where people set down their cups of tea, so it literally holds them up.

clue.text: If this craft pint was drunk, one might get narcoleptic

indicators.note: a drunk person's movements are jumbled, so the combined letters are scrambled
the clue asks what, joined with something else, would rearrange into a word, so that extra must be taken away from it

parts.note: the word whose letters are the answer plus the drink
taken as written; these letters come off

explanation.surface: A boozy warning that downing a craft beer might make you nod off.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: CORACLE plus PINT shuffle to NARCOLEPTIC. 'Craft pint' reads as craft beer, but craft is the boat and pint stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A coracle is a small round Welsh or Irish boat made of wickerwork, and any boat is a craft.

clue.text: Frustrated wearing metallic jacket

definitions.meaning: first meaning: thwarted, prevented from succeeding
second meaning: wrapped in thin sheet metal

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a shiny jacket is fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one sentence it is about a person in a jacket, but the two parts are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To be thwarted is to have plans blocked, while food wrapped in thin aluminium sheeting has been covered that way.

clue.text: Recall knowing dreary work of French artist

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the whole string runs backwards

parts.note: sage means wise or knowing
a drag is a tedious chore
de is French for of

explanation.surface: Remembering a gloomy painting by a French artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of French' looks like it describes the artist; it is the French word DE. The whole string SAGE DRAG DE is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: The French Impressionist painter famous for his ballet dancers is a celebrated example of a nineteenth-century painter.

clue.text: Container of paste perhaps endlessly swelling

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a swollen underground stem, like a potato

explanation.surface: A jar of paste keeps swelling without end.
explanation.walkthrough: TUBER loses its last letter. 'Perhaps' marks toothpaste or glue as just one example of what such a container holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothpaste, glue and tomato concentrate are all sold in squeezable cylinders, so this holder suits them.

clue.text: Blissful win against Hearts in Fife — nice!

parts.note: to beat is to win against

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters
the two central letters

explanation.surface: A Scottish football fan delights in a win over Heart of Midlothian, the Edinburgh club known as Hearts, played in Fife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearts' looks like the football club; it asks for the middle letters of both Fife and nice. Fife is a Scottish county.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatific describes an expression of serene joy, as of a saint, which matches a state of supreme happiness.

clue.text: Occasionally, mean panto character gets good in play at late stage

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens only now and then, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters

indicators.note: to get something is to take it in, so one piece receives another

parts.note: the pantomime dame is a stock comic role played by a man in drag
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A nasty pantomime villain turns good near the end of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: G goes inside DAME after its D. A pantomime is a British Christmas stage show, and the dame is its cross-dressed comic lead.
explanation.definitionFit: The endgame is the final phase of a chess match, when few pieces remain, hence the closing part of any contest.

clue.text: Information for golfer, man putting

parts.note: par is the standard score for a hole, which a golfer needs to know
a king is a man, or piece, in chess

explanation.surface: A golfer on the green gets information while lining up a putt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' looks like golf; it means placing a vehicle. A chessman is called a man, so the king is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaving a car in a space is to put it somewhere, as in putting the car in the garage.

clue.text: Historical work showing supernatural being, strange incarnation of deity

parts.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian mythology
odd means strange
Rama is an avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu

explanation.surface: A history book features a ghost and an odd earthly form of a god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an anagram signal, but it simply means ODD. PERI and RAMA are crossword regulars from Persian and Hindu tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: A costume piece for stage or screen set in an earlier era is a story from the past.

clue.text: Second-rate run that's part of football

parts.note: B grade is second class
a ladder is a run in tights or stockings

explanation.surface: A poor run that forms part of a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' sounds like a footballer's sprint, but it is a ladder in tights. 'Football' is the ball itself, not the game.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional leather ball has an inflatable inner bag of rubber inside it, holding the air.

clue.text: Soldiers, first-years in America ultimately want renewed vigour

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
American students in their first year are called freshmen

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: Army recruits and new American students crave a fresh burst of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: RE for the Royal Engineers is a standard abbreviation for soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Being refreshed restores strength and energy, so refreshment can mean a revival of liveliness, not only food and drink.

clue.text: Study of projectiles, tons found in garden area

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it

parts.note: a rockery is a part of a garden built with stones and plants
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: Heavy shells land by the ton in someone's garden.
explanation.walkthrough: T goes between the E and R of ROCKERY.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocketry is the science of designing and launching rockets, which are self-propelled missiles flying through the air.

clue.text: Some offal I placed around Asian dish

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so read the letters backwards
only some of the words are used, so the letters lie inside the run of text

parts.note: read right to left, the letters run across the words

explanation.surface: A cook arranges some offal around a plate of Asian food.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'offal I placed' backwards, PILAFF appears from the L of placed to the F of offal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilaff is rice cooked in stock with spices, a dish from Turkey, Persia and India.

clue.text: Performing flea acrobatically leaving palm wound up elsewhere on hand

indicators.note: an acrobat tumbles and twists, so the letters are thrown into a new order
whatever is leaving goes away, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters come out

explanation.surface: A circus flea tumbles off someone's palm and ends up on another part of the hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P, A, L, M from PERFORMING FLEA and rearrange the rest. 'Wound up' means ended up, linking the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The palm is part of the hand; the index finger is another part of the hand away from it.

clue.text: Respect adversary finally following award

parts.note: the Order of the British Empire, an honour given by the monarch

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: closing letter

explanation.surface: A sportsman shows respect to an opponent after receiving an honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' places the Y after OBE, a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: To respect a rule or law is to comply with it and follow what it says, as in respecting a speed limit.

clue.text: Originally develop piece without outsiders for early vehicle

indicators.note: with no outsiders, only the inner part remains, so the end letters go
done originally means made in a new way, so the letters are freshly arranged

parts.note: taken as written
piece minus its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An inventor first develops a part for a pioneering vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Originally' looks like a first-letter signal; it is the anagram signal. Only 'piece' loses its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The velocipede was the nineteenth-century forerunner of the bicycle, pedalled by its rider.

clue.text: Worker is taking up plan dealing with junk

parts.note: the worker ant
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken up means lifted bottom to top, so the letters run upwards

parts.note: a plan of an area is a map

explanation.surface: An employee adopts a scheme for getting rid of rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junk' looks like household rubbish, but it is junk email.
explanation.definitionFit: Antispam software filters unwanted bulk email messages, the kind commonly called junk mail.

clue.text: Detective with source catching criminal gang at liberty

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so the letters are bent out of order

parts.note: a Detective Inspector

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a seed is the source from which something grows
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective with an informant catches a criminal gang that had been on the loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source' looks like a police informant, but it is SEED. DI, Detective Inspector, is a common British police rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone disengaged is free from commitments, which matches being free and available.

clue.text: Casual characters around bar are dishevelled

indicators.note: letters moved around are put into a different order
dishevelled means untidy and messed up, so the letters are disordered
bar means except, so those letters are left out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters come out

explanation.surface: Laid-back types at the bar look scruffy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people and 'bar' like a pub; remove A, R, E from CHARACTERS and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A scratch team is assembled hastily and informally, so the word means improvised or makeshift.

clue.text: Approach American pub hosts

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: PH, public house, is the map abbreviation for a pub
US is short for American

explanation.surface: Someone walks up to an American bar that hosts events.
explanation.walkthrough: PH is the Ordnance Survey map label for a public house.
explanation.definitionFit: To be pushing forty is to be nearing that age, so the verb can mean getting close to.

clue.text: Free having tunnelled regularly when back in Belmarsh

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is taken

parts.note: the even-placed letters
as means when

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so its last letter is used

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A prisoner breaks out of Belmarsh, a high-security London prison, by digging a tunnel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in' looks like returning to prison; it means the end letter of Belmarsh.
explanation.definitionFit: To unleash a dog is to let it off the lead, so the verb means to release.

clue.text: Everything beginning to trouble serf

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: opening letter
a helot was a serf in ancient Sparta

explanation.surface: A medieval landowner troubles his peasant over everything.
explanation.walkthrough: HELOT, a Spartan serf, is a crossword stalwart.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal idiom for the whole amount, every single item without exception.

clue.text: Skilful as one drives in Paris losing tail

indicators.note: losing a tail means the end is cut off, so the final letter goes

parts.note: the French drive on the right, à droite

explanation.surface: A deft motorist in Paris has a car that lost its rear end.
explanation.walkthrough: À DROITE is French for on the right, the side French drivers keep to; drop its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit means dexterous and clever, from the French for to the right, the hand traditionally favoured.

clue.text: Woman's misery being surrounded by rodents

indicators.note: to be surrounded is to sit inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: mice are rodents
hell is misery or torment

explanation.surface: A woman is miserable because rats and mice are all around her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misery' looks like the woman's mood in the surface, but it supplies the inner letters; the definition is just 'Woman'.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name is a common crossword way of defining a woman, so any girl's name fits.

clue.text: Passes through centre of Tewkesbury

parts.note: by means through, as in by means of

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters

explanation.surface: Someone drives straight through the middle of Tewkesbury, an English market town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passes through' reads as a phrase, but the definition is 'Passes' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: In a tournament, competitors who skip a round without playing are given byes, free passes to the next stage.

clue.text: A university notice about year for examination

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to spot is to notice
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A university posts a notice about the year's exams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a noun, a posted sign, but it is the verb SPOT, which is reversed. 'Examination' is medical, not academic.
explanation.definitionFit: An autopsy is a post-mortem, the medical inspection of a body to find the cause of death.

clue.text: Noble's effrontery with underclothing stripped

indicators.note: something stripped has its outer layer removed, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: gall means cheek or impudence
pants is British English for underpants

explanation.surface: An aristocrat brazenly strips off his underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: PANTS loses its outer letters to leave ANT; in Britain pants are underpants, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallant describes chivalrous, honourable and brave conduct, the qualities associated with nobility.

clue.text: End of course in term

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
a stretch is a prison term

explanation.surface: The end of a course of study comes within the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' looks academic, but it is a racecourse. 'In' is a whole word, at home.
explanation.definitionFit: The final straight before the finishing line of a racetrack is the last section of the race.
